title: Midnight Type at the Lantern Press

passage.title: Midnight Type at the Lantern Press
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Thomas pulled the heavy wool cloak across the narrow cellar window in the back of Master Edes's Boston print shop. Outside on Queen Street, the boots of British patrol soldiers clicked against the wet cobblestones in the April chill. It was past midnight in 1775, and a strict curfew required every apprentice to be asleep in the loft above. Yet Master Edes had sprained his wrist that afternoon when a crate of lead bars slipped from a cart. If the urgent town broadside was going to reach the morning riders by dawn, Thomas had to set the metal type himself.

A single tallow candle flickered beside the wooden type case, casting long shadows over the tiny compartments of letters. Because metal blocks print backward on paper, each word had to be built upside down and from right to left in the brass composing stick. Working with ink-stained thumbs beside the dim flame, the reversed lead letters for the warning headline were carefully scrutinized by the young apprentice. One swapped letter could turn a solemn notice about supply wagons into a confusing jumble. Thomas breathed slowly. He checked every capital letter with the tip of his fingernail.

Upstairs, a loud knock rattled the oak street door and made the candle flame jump. Master Edes limped into the front room with his arm in a sling to speak with the sergeant. Down in the cellar, Thomas froze beside the iron press and tried to conceal the damp stack of blank paper beneath a canvas sack. Through the boards, he heard the soldier ask why a light still burned in the shop. Master Edes calmly replied that he was soaking his swollen wrist in warm salt water so he could print shipping forms at noon.

For ten tense seconds, the heavy boots paced right above Thomas's head near the cellar trapdoor. Thomas gripped the heavy iron lever of the press. He knew that a single creak of the wooden frame would give him away. At last, the street door latched shut and the patrol marched down the lane toward the harbor. Thomas let out his breath and wiped a bead of sweat from his chin.

Working twice as fast now, he locked the frame of lead type onto the flat bed of the press. He rolled the leather ink balls across the metal letters until they shone like black glass. Then he pulled the long wooden bar with all his weight. The press pushed the damp sheet against the inked type. When he peeled back the first crisp broadside, his quiet act of defiance stood bold and clear in wet black ink.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Working with ink-stained thumbs beside the dim flame, the reversed lead letters for the warning headline were carefully scrutinized by the young apprentice."

Based on the structure of this sentence, who or what is performing the action of scrutinizing?

options.text: The reversed lead letters for the warning headline
options.childFeedback: The reversed lead letters are the metal blocks being checked; inanimate metal letters cannot scrutinize (examine) anything!

options.text: The British patrol sergeant inspecting the shop
options.childFeedback: The British patrol sergeant is outside on the street in Paragraph 1 and upstairs in Paragraph 3—he never sees the lead letters in the cellar.

options.text: The dim flame flickering next to the wooden type case
options.childFeedback: The dim candle flame only provides light beside the wooden type case; the young apprentice is the person examining the letters.

options.text: The young apprentice working beside the candle
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'were carefully scrutinized by the young apprentice' shows that the young apprentice (Thomas) is the one closely examining the reversed lead letters.

questions.provingSentenceText: Working with ink-stained thumbs beside the dim flame, the reversed lead letters for the warning headline were carefully scrutinized by the young apprentice.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'were carefully scrutinized by the young apprentice' shows that the young apprentice (Thomas) is the one closely examining the reversed lead letters.
questions.parentExplanation: Because this sentence is written in passive voice ('were carefully scrutinized by the young apprentice'), the grammatical subject ('the reversed lead letters') receives the action. The true actor performing the inspection is 'the young apprentice' (Option D).
questions.retryHint: Check the words 'scrutinized by' at the end of the Paragraph 2 sentence to see who is doing the careful checking.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"Down in the cellar, Thomas froze beside the iron press and tried to conceal the damp stack of blank paper beneath a canvas sack."

What does the word "conceal" mean as it is used in this sentence?

options.text: To keep something hidden from view
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, 'conceal' means to keep something hidden from view, because Thomas puts a canvas sack over the blank paper so the British sergeant won't see it.

options.text: To dry wet sheets of paper near a candle
options.childFeedback: Colonial printers actually damped paper on purpose so it would take ink well (as seen in Paragraph 5); Thomas was hiding the stack under a sack, not drying it.

options.text: To fold a printed broadside into a neat square
options.childFeedback: The paper in Paragraph 3 is still a stack of blank sheets before printing, and Thomas is covering it under a canvas sack to hide it.

options.text: To destroy all the paper in the print shop forever
options.childFeedback: Thomas needs that paper to print the urgent broadside in Paragraph 5, so he is hiding the stack temporarily, not destroying it.

questions.provingSentenceText: Down in the cellar, Thomas froze beside the iron press and tried to conceal the damp stack of blank paper beneath a canvas sack.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, 'conceal' means to keep something hidden from view, because Thomas puts a canvas sack over the blank paper so the British sergeant won't see it.
questions.parentExplanation: The phrase 'beneath a canvas sack' while hiding in the cellar from the patrol sergeant provides a clear context clue that 'conceal' means to hide from view (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Picture why Thomas puts the damp stack of paper 'beneath a canvas sack' right when the patrol soldier knocks on the shop door.

questions.prompt: In Paragraph 3, how do Master Edes's actions upstairs help Thomas complete his task in the cellar?

options.text: Master Edes asks the patrol sergeant to help print shipping forms for the harbor at noon.
options.childFeedback: Master Edes only mentions printing shipping forms at noon as part of his cover story for soaking his wrist; he never asks the British sergeant to help print.

options.text: Master Edes carries the heavy crate of lead bars down the cellar stairs so Thomas can work faster.
options.childFeedback: Master Edes had sprained his wrist that afternoon and had his arm in a sling upstairs, so he could not carry heavy lead crates down the stairs.

options.text: Master Edes gives a calm excuse about his injured wrist that convinces the sergeant to leave without searching the cellar.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, Master Edes calmly tells the sergeant that the light is on because he is soaking his swollen wrist, which satisfies the soldier so he leaves without checking the cellar.

options.text: Master Edes locks the patrol soldiers inside the front room until the morning riders arrive.
options.childFeedback: Master Edes does not lock the soldiers in the room; Paragraph 4 states that the patrol latched the street door shut and marched away down the lane.

questions.provingSentenceText: Master Edes calmly replied that he was soaking his swollen wrist in warm salt water so he could print shipping forms at noon.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, Master Edes calmly tells the sergeant that the light is on because he is soaking his swollen wrist, which satisfies the soldier so he leaves without checking the cellar.
questions.parentExplanation: Aligned to ELAGSE5RL3 (how characters interact and respond to challenges), Master Edes protects Thomas's secret work below by using his real wrist injury as a believable excuse for why a light is burning past curfew (Option C).
questions.retryHint: Read the last two sentences of Paragraph 3 to see what Master Edes says to explain why a light is still burning in the shop.

questions.prompt: How does Paragraph 4 contribute to the overall structure of the story?

options.text: It proves that Thomas was too frightened to ever touch the printing press again.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 5 shows the exact opposite: as soon as the soldiers leave, Thomas works twice as fast to ink the type and pull the press lever.

options.text: It explains the historical rules for how apprentices were hired in colonial Boston.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 describes the ten tense seconds of the patrol pacing above the trapdoor, not historical hiring rules for Boston apprentices.

options.text: It introduces the main conflict by showing how Master Edes sprained his wrist on the cart.
options.childFeedback: Master Edes's sprained wrist and the main problem of printing the notice before dawn are introduced back in Paragraph 1, not Paragraph 4.

options.text: It builds the story's highest moment of suspense as the patrol boots pace right above Thomas's hiding spot before leaving.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 creates the story's peak moment of suspense as the soldier's heavy boots pace right above the cellar trapdoor while Thomas holds his breath beside the silent press.

questions.provingSentenceText: For ten tense seconds, the heavy boots paced right above Thomas's head near the cellar trapdoor.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 4 creates the story's peak moment of suspense as the soldier's heavy boots pace right above the cellar trapdoor while Thomas holds his breath beside the silent press.
questions.parentExplanation: Aligned to ELAGSE5RL5, Paragraph 4 serves as the climax of tension between the sergeant's arrival in Paragraph 3 and the triumphant printing resolution in Paragraph 5 (Option D).
questions.retryHint: Notice how Paragraph 4 counts 'ten tense seconds' while the patrol boots pace right above Thomas's head before finally marching away.

questions.prompt: PART A: What can the reader infer about setting metal type on a colonial printing press from Paragraph 2?

options.text: It required intense focus and patience because letters had to be placed backward and checked one by one.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 shows that setting type demanded intense focus and patience because the metal letters printed backward, forcing Thomas to build each word upside down and right to left.

options.text: It could only be done in total darkness because candle heat melted the lead letters.
options.childFeedback: Thomas works right beside a burning tallow candle in Paragraph 2; a small candle flame does not melt lead type.

options.text: It was the easiest job in the print shop and required no training to master.
options.childFeedback: Setting backward metal type in dim light was so tricky that a single swapped letter could turn the notice into a confusing jumble, so it was far from easy.

options.text: It used brass composing sticks that automatically corrected spelling mistakes.
options.childFeedback: The brass composing stick was just a hand tool that held the metal letters; Thomas had to check every capital letter himself with the tip of his fingernail.

questions.provingSentenceText: Because metal blocks print backward on paper, each word had to be built upside down and from right to left in the brass composing stick.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 2 shows that setting type demanded intense focus and patience because the metal letters printed backward, forcing Thomas to build each word upside down and right to left.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 describes how metal type prints in reverse, requiring the printer to assemble words upside down and right-to-left while checking every character so a swapped letter wouldn't garble the message (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Reread Paragraph 2 to see how each word had to be arranged in the brass composing stick and why one swapped letter would cause trouble.

questions.prompt: PART B: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "Outside on Queen Street, the boots of British patrol soldiers clicked against the wet cobblestones in the April chill."
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 1 sets the midnight scene on Queen Street, without explaining the careful skill needed to set metal type.

options.text: "Because metal blocks print backward on paper, each word had to be built upside down and from right to left in the brass composing stick."
options.childFeedback: This quotation from Paragraph 2 directly proves Question 5 by explaining why setting type was so demanding: every word had to be built upside down and from right to left.

options.text: "Upstairs, a loud knock rattled the oak street door and made the candle flame jump."
options.childFeedback: This line from Paragraph 3 describes the soldier knocking on the door upstairs, not the process of arranging metal letters in the composing stick.

options.text: "He rolled the leather ink balls across the metal letters until they shone like black glass."
options.childFeedback: This detail from Paragraph 5 describes rolling ink across the finished frame, after all the difficult backward letter-setting in Paragraph 2 was already done.

questions.provingSentenceText: Because metal blocks print backward on paper, each word had to be built upside down and from right to left in the brass composing stick.
questions.childTip: This quotation from Paragraph 2 directly proves Question 5 by explaining why setting type was so demanding: every word had to be built upside down and from right to left.
questions.parentExplanation: Option B directly proves the inference in Part A by detailing the backward, upside-down, right-to-left precision required to set metal type.
